subject: anatomy
title: Femoral Triangle, Femoral Sheath, and Femoral Canal Anatomy

steps.tx: The femoral triangle (Scarpa triangle) is a triangular subfascial depression located in the upper third of the anterior thigh. Its base is formed superiorly by the **inguinal ligament**, its lateral border by the medial margin of sartorius, and its medial border by the medial margin of adductor longus.
steps.say: The femoral triangle is a subfascial space in the upper anterior thigh. Superiorly, the inguinal ligament forms its base, while the medial margin of sartorius forms its lateral boundary and adductor longus forms its medial boundary.

rows: Meeting of Sartorius and Adductor Longus
Guides vascular entry into Hunter canal

steps.tx: The contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial are the femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, and deep inguinal lymphatics. Crucially, the **femoral nerve** lies directly on the iliopsoas muscle outside the femoral sheath, separated from the femoral artery by the deep iliopectineal fascia.
steps.say: From lateral to medial, the contents of the femoral triangle are the femoral nerve, artery, vein, and lymphatic channel. Notably, the femoral nerve rests outside the femoral sheath, partitioned from the artery by iliopectineal fascia.

left.title: Outside Femoral Sheath (Lateral)
points: Divides into anterior and posterior divisions
Free from sheath entrapment or hernia

right.title: Inside Femoral Sheath (Medial)
points: Lateral compartment: femoral artery and genitofemoral branch
Medial compartment: femoral canal and lymphatics

steps.tx: The **femoral sheath** is a funnel-shaped fascial sleeve extending approximately three to four centimeters below the inguinal ligament. Formed by downward prolongation of abdominal transversalis fascia anteriorly and iliac fascia posteriorly, it fuses distally with the adventitia of the femoral vessels.
steps.say: The femoral sheath is a funnel of connective tissue extending four centimeters into the upper thigh. Formed by abdominal fascia transversalis anteriorly and fascia iliaca posteriorly, it blends distally into vessel adventitia.

nodes.label: Abdominal Fascia Transversalis and Fascia Iliaca Descend
Funnel-shaped Femoral Sheath Surrounds Vascular Inflow
Lateral: Femoral Artery and Lumboinguinal Nerve
Medial: Femoral Canal (1.25 cm Dead Space)

steps.tx: The medial compartment of the femoral sheath is the conical **femoral canal**, measuring approximately 1.25 centimetres in length. It contains loose adipose tissue, efferent lymphatics, and the deep inguinal lymph node of Cloquet (Rosenmuller). Its physiological function is to provide dead space allowing the adjacent femoral vein to expand during exercise.
steps.say: The medial compartment of the sheath is the femoral canal, roughly one and a quarter centimeters long. Containing fat and Cloquet lymph node, it provides physiological space for femoral vein distension during exertion.

vis.alt: Cross section of femoral sheath showing lateral, intermediate, and medial femoral canal compartments
vis.caption: Anatomical cross-section of the femoral sheath compartments and boundaries of the femoral ring. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The upper abdominal opening of the femoral canal is the **femoral ring**. Its boundaries are rigid and unforgiving: bounded anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, posteriorly by the pectineus muscle and pectineal ligament of Astley Cooper, medially by the crescentic margin of the lacunar ligament of Gimbernat, and laterally by the femoral vein.
steps.say: The proximal entrance to the femoral canal is the femoral ring. It has rigid boundaries: the inguinal ligament anteriorly, Cooper pectineal ligament posteriorly, sharp lacunar ligament medially, and femoral vein laterally.

rows: Cannot be divided without hernia recurrence
Site of stridor; divide carefully to relieve strangulation
Avoid lateral cuts to prevent catastrophic venous tear

steps.tx: A **femoral hernia** occurs when abdominal viscera protrude through the femoral ring into the femoral canal, emerging through the cribriform fascia of the saphenous opening into subcutaneous tissue. Presenting as a groin mass below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, it occurs much more frequently in females due to a wider pelvis.
steps.say: A femoral hernia develops when abdominal contents enter the femoral canal and emerge through the saphenous opening. Presenting below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, it affects women more frequently due to a broader pelvic architecture.

vis.alt: Anatomical landmarks distinguishing indirect, direct, and femoral hernia orifices
vis.caption: Groin hernia orifices illustrating the position of the femoral canal relative to the inguinal canal. [Credit: Dennis M. DePace, PhD / Wikimedia Commons]

steps.tx: Because the boundaries of the femoral ring are rigid—particularly the sharp medial margin of the lacunar ligament—femoral hernias have the highest rate of **strangulation** of all groin hernias. When relieving a strangulated femoral hernia, incising the lacunar ligament medially risks dividing an abnormal obturator artery present in thirty percent of individuals.
steps.say: Because its boundaries are unyielding, particularly the lacunar ligament, femoral hernias carry an exceptionally high risk of strangulation. Relieving constriction by cutting medially risks lacerating an accessory obturator artery.

left.title: Femoral Hernia
points: Neck lies below and lateral to pubic tubercle
Emerges through femoral ring and canal

right.title: Inguinal Hernia
points: Neck lies above and medial to pubic tubercle
Lower immediate risk of acute strangulation

steps.tx: Distally, the femoral triangle continues directly into the **adductor canal** (Hunter canal or subsartorial canal). This aponeurotic tunnel in the middle third of the medial thigh extends from the apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus, conducting the femoral artery, femoral vein, saphenous nerve, and nerve to vastus medialis.
steps.say: At its apex, the femoral triangle transitions into the adductor canal of Hunter. Located in the middle third of the thigh, this aponeurotic tunnel transmits the femoral artery, femoral vein, saphenous nerve, and nerve to vastus medialis.
